extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, researchers, and readers interested in research integrity and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards used by journals and institutions to evaluate whether published research should be retracted for ethical or methodological failings; includes specific ethical failings identified by an institutional investigation and editorial decision-making practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: COPE guideline: retract if it reports unethical research
rubrics_metrics.description: In line with the Committee on Publication Ethics Guidelines for Retractions recommending that “Editors should consider retracting a publication if […] it reports unethical research.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should treat confirmed instances of unethical research as legitimate grounds for retraction; re-evaluation of cases can be guided by COPE recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of any biological hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Karolinska Institutet found that the research “lacked any biological hypothesis based on either in vitro or in vivo (animal) data.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A study without a clearly articulated biological hypothesis (and supporting preclinical rationale) undermines scientific validity and can constitute unethical research warranting corrective action or retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of documented advance discussion of risks and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: The notebook also lacks notes on any advance discussion of the risks and benefits of the treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to document risk–benefit deliberations for experimental treatments indicates lack of ethical oversight and informed consideration, and is a serious ethical deficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: No stated theory underpinning the treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The notebook lacks the theory on which [the treatment] was based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research should state the theoretical rationale for interventions; absence of such theory suggests poor scientific foundation and ethical problems in justifying human experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: No preclinical or other studies demonstrating effect or safety
rubrics_metrics.description: The notebook lacks the results of preclinical or other studies demonstrating effect, and safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceeding to experimental treatments in humans without preclinical evidence of effect and safety breaches standard research ethics and clinical trial norms and can justify retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to document discussion after patient deterioration and unjustified continuation
rubrics_metrics.description: No discussion that followed from the deterioration of the patient’s condition, in spite of which it was decided to continue the experimental treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuing experimental interventions after adverse outcomes without documented re-assessment or justification is an ethical violation and supports corrective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contravention of Declaration of Helsinki provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Karolinska found the conduct “contravenes articles 14, 16, 17, and 21 of the 2013 Declaration of Helsinki (articles 31, 21, 18, and 12 of the 2008 version).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations of the Declaration of Helsinki (key international ethical standards for research involving human subjects) are strong grounds for retraction and institutional sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical permit present but underlying research not ethically conducted
rubrics_metrics.description: According to Karolinska Institute, although the 2015 paper included an ethical permit, the underlying research did not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession of a documented permit does not by itself prove ethical conduct; journals and institutions should verify that approved protocols were followed and that documentation matches actual practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial decision process: conduct independent analysis and consider all available information
rubrics_metrics.description: Editor: “In any retraction case we conduct our own analysis and consider all available information. In this specific case we needed to consider four other renowned institutions besides KI and the 26 authors of the article.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should perform their own assessment, weigh external institutional reports and author responses, and consider the full body of evidence before deciding whether to retract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of transparency (publishing statements) versus retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal previously stated it saw itself as a forum and aimed ‘by publishing the different statements including KI’s report concerning the article our aim is to make the conflict completely transparent.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may initially opt to publish competing statements to expose conflicts and evidence, but transparency alone may be insufficient when independent investigations demonstrate ethical breaches—retraction may still be appropriate on re-evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author agreement or non-response noted in retraction decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notice: ‘Ana I. Teixeira, Adil Duru and Vanessa Lundin agree with this retraction. The remaining authors did not respond or could not be reached for comment within the timeframe given.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noting author agreement or lack of response is part of the retraction process; lack of unanimous author consent does not prevent retraction when ethical breaches are established.
